reading.body:
Profit Finder Pro Software is not a data center. It is a customer relationship management and sales-tracking product for roofing, solar, contracting, and insurance businesses, listed at a Scottsdale, Arizona address that another company now occupies.

The entry exists because an OpenStreetMap point was tagged telecom=data_center. No specifications are published, and research across the available sources found no connection between the company, the address, and any server infrastructure, colocation space, or dedicated data center equipment. The stored coordinates resolve to a different current occupant several miles from the other eight rows in the same batch, so no single shared building links them. Each appears to be an independently mistagged small business scattered across the Phoenix metro.

That matters for AI infrastructure accounting because capacity totals are assembled from lists like this one. Arizona's published figure of 512 MW across four facilities with published numbers is unaffected by this entry, which carries zero megawatts. But the same tagging process that produced this spurious point also produced the entries that do carry megawatts, and a mistag is only caught when someone checks an address against ground truth.

What the data does not show is how often that check fails. It gives no count of other mistagged points, no independent verification of the four Arizona facilities that do report capacity, and no measurement of actual power draw or grid load anywhere. It establishes one thing: this address is not part of AI's power demand and should not be counted as such.
